name: Talos Linux
license: MPL 2.0 (Omni, its management platform, is source-available under BUSL 1.1)
summary: A Linux distribution that only runs Kubernetes: immutable, minimal, with no shell or SSH, and managed entirely through an API.
intro: Talos Linux keeps the Linux kernel and replaces everything above it with its own components written in Go. PID 1 is `machined`, not systemd, and it won’t start arbitrary services. There is no shell, no SSH, no package manager and none of the GNU utilities; the whole OS is a signed SquashFS image under 80 MB that is mounted read-only into memory, even when installed to disk. The only writable state is a few files under `/system` that are rebuilt on each boot and an XFS partition at `/var` for etcd, the kubelet and containerd, which Talos treats as disposable.

Every machine is described by one YAML machine config, covering both the OS and the Kubernetes it forms. You manage nodes with `talosctl`, which talks to an encrypted, key-authenticated gRPC API (`apid`) on each node: apply a config, read logs, reboot, upgrade, bootstrap etcd. Upgrades swap in a new OS image with an A-B scheme and roll back automatically if the new one doesn’t boot. Drivers and extra tools come as system extensions baked into the image, for example by Sidero’s Image Factory. Omni, Sidero’s cluster manager, adds a UI, single sign-on and fleet-wide upgrades as a SaaS or self-hosted, but under a source-available licence that requires a paid licence for production.
strengths: Tiny attack surface: no shell, SSH or passwords, a kernel hardened along Kernel Self Protection Project lines, and fewer than 50 binaries by Sidero’s count
Nodes are cattle: one declarative config per role, and any node can be wiped and rebuilt from it
Atomic A-B upgrades with automatic rollback, driven by API calls you can script
Runs the same on AWS, Azure, GCP and about ten other clouds, on VMware, Proxmox and bare metal, and on boards like the Raspberry Pi 4
limits: No shell means debugging is different: you inspect nodes through `talosctl` API calls such as `dmesg` and `memory`, and anything a node needs must be in the image or the config
Community support for a release ends when the next minor release ships, about every four months; enterprise support comes from Sidero Labs
FIPS-compliant builds, SBOMs per build, CVE SLAs and indemnity are only in the paid Talos Enterprise Linux licence
A node in maintenance mode accepts an unauthenticated config by design, so first boot needs a trusted network or a config supplied at boot

snippet.title: Turn a machine booted from the Talos ISO into a one-node control plane
source: # generate controlplane.yaml, worker.yaml and talosconfig (client credentials)
# the node waits in maintenance mode for its config
talosctl bootstrap --nodes $CONTROL_PLANE_IP --talosconfig=./talosconfig   # once, on one node

story: Talos began as a nights-and-weekends project by Andrew Rynhard, who was tired of automating the same general-purpose Linux servers over and over. His question was what an operating system would look like if it existed only to run Kubernetes. The repository dates from late 2017 and the first alpha release from April 2018. Container-optimised systems such as CoreOS already existed, but in Rynhard’s view they still carried the baggage of general-purpose Linux.

Talos Systems launched as a company in June 2019 to support it, planning to sell services, support and management tools. A trademark clash with Cisco’s Talos security group led it to rename itself Sidero Labs in October 2021, while the OS kept the Talos name. Talos 1.0 followed in March 2022. Omni, a hosted manager for Talos clusters, came next; in February 2024 Sidero published its source under the Business Source License so people could self-host it for non-production use.

In September 2026 Yardi, a large private software company that ran Talos in production, acquired Sidero Labs. Sidero said Talos stays MPL-2.0 and the company keeps operating independently, and the next day launched Talos Enterprise Linux, a commercial licence for compliance artifacts and FIPS builds.

choices.choice: An API instead of a shell
choices.why: Logging into nodes to fix them by hand makes servers drift apart. With no console or SSH, every change goes through one authenticated, declarative API, so nodes built from the same config stay identical.

Trimming an existing distribution still leaves its init system, utilities and libraries. Writing `machined` and the other services in Go meant shipping only what Kubernetes needs, so there are far fewer packages to patch and vulnerabilities to track.

choices.choice: Run from a read-only image, keep state ephemeral
choices.why: Because the OS is one signed SquashFS image and the writable partition holds only replicated or rebuildable data, a broken node can be wiped and rebuilt from its config, and its image can be checked for tampering.
Upgrading a whole image instead of packages means each node runs a known, tested version. Keeping the previous image lets a node that fails to boot fall back automatically.
